themes.name: No Ground Truth to Measure Against
themes.plain: Most of these problems have no answer key. There is no stable number to grade your work against, and the thing you are measuring often changes while you measure it, so the models start by building a small truth set of their own or admit the number is only an estimate.
themes.evidence: On answer engine optimization the models all start by logging thousands of real buyer questions because answers are personalized and shifting; on cross-channel incrementality they run always-on holdouts because platforms adapt to the test; on identity resolution they recruit consenting people as a truth set; on B2B buying-group signal loss they say a lost signal and a never-real signal look identical.

themes.name: Chokepoint Before Trust
themes.plain: When the models cannot trust who is acting or what will happen next, they build one door they own and push everything through it. A sent email, a spent dollar, or an exported file cannot be taken back, so the only real control happens before the action leaves.
themes.evidence: On safe agent execution every model puts a proxy or gateway in front of martech writes with hard spend and audience caps; on downstream consent and deletion they inventory every path data leaves the building, including manual exports, and force each one through a single checkpoint.

themes.name: Nobody Can Verify Downstream
themes.plain: Once data, a message, or a dollar leaves your own systems, you cannot see inside the partner, ad platform, or trained model that now holds it. You can watch from outside and estimate whether the rules were followed, but you cannot prove it.
themes.evidence: Today's answers on downstream consent and deletion all end at the same wall: ad networks and trained model weights are black boxes with no person-level removal proof, so Claude falls back on signed evidence plus planted canary identities; the same opacity shows up in ad supply integrity and in incrementality, where platforms control both the treatment and the evidence.

themes.name: Incentives Before Standards
themes.plain: Many of these problems stall because the people who hold the answer gain nothing by sharing it, and nobody can force them. The blockers are money and politics, inside the company as much as outside, so the models try to make honesty or cooperation pay rather than write another rule.
themes.evidence: On agentic traffic all three models build a fast lane with better prices or data so declaring beats spoofing, and name liability and adoption as harder than the protocol; on journey orchestration the blocker is channel owners whose bonuses reward sending; on ad supply integrity the open market is described as addicted to fake volume.

themes.name: Judgment That Won't Compile
themes.plain: The hardest calls turn on meaning and context: whether a picture plus a headline implies a promise, whether evidence really backs a claim, whether two teams can both be right about what a word means. No rule set captures that, so the models shrink human judgment into a smaller, safer box instead of removing it.
themes.evidence: On generative content governance all three models build a registry of pre-approved claims and restrict generation to it, because implied meaning is what review actually catches; on the semantic context layer they report that conflicting definitions of customer are a political settlement, not a modeling gap.
